description.narrative: TThis programme is being developed in an economy that is starting to recover from the sharp shock it experienced due to the negative impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and the measures instituted to curb it. The demand for Uganda’s exports has dwindled, remittancesfrom the diaspora have dried up, Foreign Direct Investment and domestic tax collections have been severely disrupted due to the stringent lockdown measures adopted by the Government of Uganda . Indeed, the economy’s growth rate has slumped to its lowest (3%), in three decades. Of particular concern is the finding that close to 2.6 million people would be pushed below the poverty line on account of this pandemic alone, if nothing is done to cushion them. On the social front, the pandemic has disrupted the delivery of basic health and education services which may have long term consequences for the country’s human capital formulation and productivity. Moreover, the Uganda Bureau of Statistics estimates that 3.8 million workers in Uganda will lose their jobs temporarily, while 625,957 will lose theirs permanently, if the threat of COVID-19 persists. Relatedly, the high unemployment rates (made worse by the pandemic), particularly among young people (estimated at 75%) due to limited industry relevant skills and a general lack of opportunity, is leading to social discontent and frustration . The limited access to productive assets by these young people, and women, limits their engagement in gainful enterprise. Furthermore, the rapid degradation and depletion of Uganda’s natural capital, particularly in the Agriculture sector, may expose the country to an increase in climatic shocks which could further undermine the livelihoods of many vulnerable communities. As alluded to earlier, the pandemic disproportionately affected SMEs. Uganda has 1,100,000 SMEs whichaccount for over 90% of Uganda’s private sector and accounting for 8,500,000 non-farm jobs . Most of the women employed in the private sector are employed by SMEs. In studies conducted by the Economic Policy Research Centre and the Federation of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises-Uganda, among others; to assess the impact of the pandemic on the sector, it was found that: micro and small scale businesses experienced a larger decline in activity compared to their larger counterparts , SMEs are experiencing reduced demand for their goods and services , liquidity and cash flow constraints, reduced production and productivity due to supply chain disruptions and staff shortages, among others. participating-org.narrative: We founded Open Capital Advisors (OCA) in 2010 to unlock growth and investment in East and Southern Africa. The creation of OCA was driven by a core gap our founders observed between businesses and investors in the region. We saw many small growing businesses (SGBs) with massive potential and opportunity for scale, but who struggled to find financing to support their growth. At the same time, we encountered investors who had available capital, but were unable to find sufficient businesses they deemed #investment ready#. The investors required a higher level of formalization and strategic planning than the businesses they currently encountered in the market. To bridge this gap OCA provides high-quality, intensive support to help our clients adapt to rapidly changing and growingmarkets, including co-designing strategies, implementing best practices, and raising external funds to drive growth and impact. We take significant risk alongside our SGB clients, typically deferring a portion of fees onto a successful capital raise. This approach allows us to work with businesses that would otherwise be unable to afford support. We have developed innovative programs with impact investors, USAID, and others to defray risk and work with even earlier-stage companies. We target SGB clients looking to raise between $500K - $5M USD. These SGBs are trying to solve the toughest problems in their local markets, including agriculture, renewable energy, financial inclusion, and more. We select SGBs where our work will help them transform markets, create new jobs, and innovate products and services. Today, Open Capital Advisors has offices incorporated in Kenya and Uganda with our team of 42 full-time professionals spread across Nairobi and Kampala. Our approach to integrating gender has evolved and expanded in focus over the maturation of the firm. We view our gender agenda as having two prongs: internal and external. Internally, we focus on hiring, training and retaining highly talented employees, especially women. As laid out in greater detail in our organogram below, over half of our entire team is female, and 50% of our senior management team (including 1 of two founding partners) is female. In 2015 we hired a dedicated head of Human Resources who has studiedgender equity in the workplace. She has helped us formalize our practices on gender equity, including updating our HR procedures and introducing a gender policy. Externally, we work with and support promising entrepreneurs, many of whom are female. Historically, 30% of the founders we have worked with have been women and we continue to focus on increasing this ratio. Further, we work with many pro-women businesses, that include empowering women # in their workforce or throughtheir products / services# as a core component of their business model.
